newsitem.title: SPAIN: Jordan King deflects blame for killing of Israelis.
newsitem.headline: Jordan King deflects blame for killing of Israelis.

text.p: Jordan's King Hussein defended himself on Thursday against accusations by Israeli ministers that he bore some responsibility for a lone Jordanian soldier's killing of seven Israeli schoolgirls.

Hussein came under fire for accusing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of pushing Arabs and Israelis towards "an abyss of bloodshed and disaster" with a plan to expand Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.

"When I warned a couple of days ago about what I perceived as a danger, the possibility of violence, I never thought that it would (turn out) the way it did today," Hussein told reporters during a private visit to Spain.
"I was fully in my responsibility to try to warn one and all that we have come too far," the king said at a Madrid palace just before bidding farewell to Spanish King Juan Carlos.
Hussein cut short his trip to Spain, a stopover on the way to Washington, and postponed the visit to the United States to fly home and deal with the fresh crisis in Middle East peace.

Before the attack, Arabs had warned Israel its plan to build housing in highly sensitive East Jerusalem had plunged the whole U.S.-sponsored Middle East peace drive into crisis. Hussein sent his warning in a letter to Netanyahu on Sunday.
Israeli Education Minister Zevulun Hammer suggested after the attack that King Hussein should not have spoken out about possible violence.
"Perhaps the conclusion is that the king must hold his tongue so that a soldier doesn't take his words to mean more than he intended," Hammer told Israel's army radio.
Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy said the gunman may have been provoked by disparaging comments about Israel but he denied he was referring to the king's letter.
"Who knows...how many of these gun-toting lunatics are waiting for the green light in the form of a remark in which Israel is described the way it is being described today," Levy said.

Seven Israeli girls were killed and at least six wounded by a Jordanian soldier who sprayed automatic gunfire at a group of 12 to 14-year-olds on a field trip to a Jordanian border site nicknamed "The Island of Peace".
It was the bloodiest attack by a Jordanian soldier on the Israel-Jordan frontier in many years.
Hussein urged Jews and Arabs to heal their wounds and pledged to work the rest of his life for Middle East peace.

"I can assure one and all that I shall do everything I can as long as I live to leave behind a legacy of peace between the descendants of the children of Abraham for all time," Hussein said before leaving Spain.
"Ours must be a way of trying to heal wounds and to build together a future worthy of us all."
Hussein said he had been troubled lately by a feeling the peace he had long worked for was facing a difficult moment.

"I hope people realise that beyond everything, there is one worthy objective and that is to seek to have a comprehensive, honourable, just peace between all our people for all time to come," Hussein said.
He said the majority of Israelis and Arabs who want peace must prevail.
"We should not let a minority of extremists, wherever they may be, dictate their agenda on us."
Hussein expressed anger and sadness at what he called a tragic loss of innocent lives.
"I sympathise with the families. I wish I could see them all and share with them in their sorrow," he said.
"This is something that is aimed I feel at me, at my children, at the people of Jordan and at the honour of the Jordanian Arab army."

Spanish King Juan Carlos and Queen Sofia, flanked by palace guards on horseback wearing armour and plumed helmets, bid King Hussein and Queen Noor farewell in a departure ceremony at Madrid's Pardo royal palace.
